when: a change adds another sibling implementation of a concept that already has others, or adds a shared base class or interface, as a loose file beside unrelated modules or beside the concrete implementations
expect: Ask the author to move the sibling implementations into a dedicated subpackage folder for that concept. Shared base classes and interfaces should go in the package's base folder, not at the package top level beside the concrete implementations.
why: Grouping each concept's implementations together and keeping its abstractions apart makes the layout navigable and the extension point obvious.
examples: PR #3359: several transfer contexts (shm.py and others) were left loose in lmcache/v1/multiprocess/; the reviewer asked for a transfer_context/ folder.
PR #4075: the base event-IPC interface was added at lmcache/v1/platform/event_ipc.py; the reviewer asked for it to live under lmcache/v1/platform/base/.
concern: Group sibling implementations and shared base abstractions into their own subpackage folders

when: a change introduces or extends a stream of events or messages that one or more producers send to a central consumer, which uses them to maintain state
expect: Require each message to carry a monotonically increasing per-producer sequence number. Require the receiver to check it so that dropped, duplicated or out-of-order messages are detected and handled.
why: Without sequence numbers the consumer cannot detect lost or reordered events, so its state can silently diverge from the producers'.
examples: PR #3630: worker-to-coordinator L2 events in lmcache/v1/mp_coordinator/l2/event_listener.py had no sequence number, so the coordinator could not check for inconsistencies.
concern: Workers-to-coordinator events carry monotonic sequence numbers

when: a change adds or modifies eviction or cache-replacement logic (victim selection, LRU-style ordering, eviction bookkeeping) in any component, such as a coordinator, backend, server or manager
expect: LMCache implements its eviction policies in lmcache/v1/distributed/eviction_policy/. Check that the change reuses one of those policies. If new behavior is needed, require the author to extend the policies there instead of writing a special-purpose eviction policy inside the component.
why: Parallel eviction implementations drift apart and duplicate bugs, tuning and tests.
examples: PR #3630: the coordinator's l2/eviction_manager.py implemented its own eviction policy instead of reusing e.g. IsolatedLRUEvictionPolicy.
concern: Reuse existing eviction policy implementations instead of writing new ones

when: a change adds or renames a configuration parameter whose name could be read as more than one quantity, or adds one setting that conflates the condition that triggers an action with how much that action does
expect: Require a name that states exactly what the value controls. Require separate, distinctly named settings for the threshold that triggers an action and for the amount that action processes.
why: A setting cannot be tuned correctly if its name does not say whether it is a trigger or a quantity, and one value cannot express both.
examples: PR #3630: EVICTION_RATIO in mp_coordinator/config.py could mean either the watermark that triggers eviction or the fraction to evict.
concern: Unambiguous config names; separate trigger threshold from action amount

when: a change extracts a few lines into a new helper function or method that has exactly one call site and no independent reuse
expect: Ask the author to inline the code into its single caller, unless the helper provides real reuse or genuinely clarifies the caller.
why: Trivial single-use helpers add indirection and spread one operation across places without adding reuse.
examples: PR #4015: the two-line _release_entry and _reclaim_device_memory helpers in lmcache_driven_transfer.py were called only from _release_entries; the reviewer asked to fold them into it.

when: a docstring or comment narrates implementation internals, bug history, reference-lifetime subtleties or type-checker appeasement, instead of stating what the caller needs to know
expect: Require docstrings to state only the high-level behavior and the caller-facing contract. Ask the author to remove mechanism and bug-history narration from docstrings and long explanatory comments from call sites. Any mechanism note that is truly needed should be at most a short inline comment at the relevant line.
why: Implementation narration buries the contract callers need and goes stale as the code changes.
examples: PR #4015: the _release_entries docstring explained CUDA-IPC unmapping, issue LMCache#4014 and rules about not binding entries to local names.
PR #4015: unregister_kv_cache had a multi-line call-site comment about why a comprehension keeps the popped entry out of local names and satisfies mypy; the reviewer asked to remove it.
concern: Keep docstrings and comments to the contract; no implementation narration

when: a change adds or modifies a public interface, Protocol or abstract base class
expect: Require a docstring on every method of the interface that states its contract. Require precise parameter and return types instead of catch-all types such as object or Any, using concrete classes, Protocols, TypeVars or unions as needed.
why: Implementers and callers code against the interface, so it must be self-documenting and type-checkable.
examples: PR #4075: EventIPCBackend methods such as create_event(device: object) -> object and export_event(event: object, device: object) -> bytes had no docstrings and typed devices, events and streams as object.
concern: Public interface methods need docstrings and precise types

when: a parameter is given an optional None default even though the function only makes sense with a real value, and the function silently falls back to an implicit global or ambient default when it is omitted
expect: Ask the author to make the parameter required and to apply this consistently across the related helper functions. Keep a None default only where None has a deliberate, documented meaning.
why: Implicit fallbacks hide caller mistakes and make behavior depend on ambient state, for example acting on the wrong device.
examples: PR #4075: get_event_ipc_backend(device: object | None = None) and similar helpers fell back to the active torch device type when no device was passed.
concern: Make needed parameters required rather than Optional with None default

when: a change adds a new source file, or substantially reorganizes one, so that private helpers, public classes and entry-point functions are mixed in arbitrary order
expect: Require this layout: imports; then private module-level helper functions and classes (prefixed `_`); then public classes, each ordered as `__init__`, public methods, then private `_` methods; then public module-level functions used by other modules.
why: A consistent layout lets readers find the public surface and its supporting helpers predictably.
examples: PR #4075: helper functions in lmcache/v1/platform/event_ipc.py were interleaved with the public protocol and entry points such as get_event_ipc_backend.

when: a change renames or replaces a public function, method or class and keeps the old name for backward compatibility
expect: LMCache provides the `@lmcache_deprecate` decorator in `lmcache.utils`. Require the old name to be kept as an explicit wrapper that delegates to the new name and is decorated with `@lmcache_deprecate`, not as a bare alias assignment. Require internal callers to be migrated to the new name.
why: A bare alias is silent: users get no deprecation signal and the old name never goes away.
examples: PR #4075: futures.py used `to_cuda_future = to_device_future` and a module-level CUDAMessagingFuture alias after the rename to DeviceMessagingFuture, instead of a `def to_cuda_future(...)` wrapper decorated with `@lmcache_deprecate`.
concern: Renamed public APIs keep the old name as a deprecated wrapper

when: a diff adds or edits a code comment, docstring, TODO, log message or error string that labels or justifies the code by pointing at context only the current PR, its plan or its discussion carries (a numbered goal, a phase or step label, a design-doc section, a ticket shorthand, 'as discussed', 'the new approach'), so a later reader with only the repository cannot tell what it means
expect: Flag every such reference and ask the author to replace it with the concrete reason the code exists, stated in terms of the code itself (what it preserves, which callers or invariant depend on it, what condition allows removing it), so the comment reads correctly from the file alone. If the outside context is really needed, ask for a stable link to a durable artifact (an issue or a committed doc) plus a one-line summary inline, never a bare label.
why: Planning labels mean nothing once the PR merges and the plan or design doc drifts or disappears, so the comment no longer explains the code to the next reader.
examples: PR #4075, lmcache/v1/multiprocess/futures.py: '# Backward-compatible alias for existing imports (Goal 3).' above `CUDAMessagingFuture = DeviceMessagingFuture`. The reviewer said nobody will understand 'Goal 3'. Drop the label and keep the real reason ('kept so existing imports of CUDAMessagingFuture keep working').
Hypothetical '# Phase 2: remove after step B lands' above a compatibility shim should instead state the removal condition, e.g. 'remove once no caller imports the old name'.
concern: Comments must be self-contained, with no PR-local planning labels

when: A change adds state or a capability (attribute, cache field, method, abstract hook) to a base class or shared base type although the base type's own implementation does not use it, or it is not inherent to what the base type represents. Typical cases: only some subclasses need it, all current subclasses happen to need it, or classes outside the hierarchy could also need it.
expect: Ask the author to keep the base type limited to state and capabilities that its own implementation uses and that every future subclass must have. If they cannot justify that, define the capability only in the subclasses that actually need it. If several classes need it, possibly including classes outside the hierarchy, put it in a separate opt-in interface, mixin or protocol, and have callers depend on that interface instead of on the base type.
why: Base types that accumulate incidental capabilities force them on future subclasses and lock out non-subclasses that need the same capability.
examples: `DeviceSpec` gained a `_event_backend_cache` attribute although the base `event_ipc_backend` returns None; reviewer asked to define the cache only in the subclasses that use it (e.g. cuda, cpu).

`get_durable_components` was added to `View` only because all existing Views implement it; reviewer asked whether every future View will need it and whether a non-View class never will, pointing toward a separate interface/mixin.

tests.note: base holds a field only some subclasses use; AI suggested the opposite (hoist caching into base)
base holds a field only some subclasses use; AI suggested the opposite (hoist caching into base)

concern: Base types hold only inherent/used capabilities; others go in subclasses or opt-in interfaces
